Policy "Parameterized SQL only":
SQL must be built with parameters or an ORM, never by concatenating or formatting strings with values that come from outside the program. Table and column names taken from constants in the code are fine.

<untrusted_code>
File: app/users.py
Lines: 15-15
Rule message: Possible violation of the policy "Parameterized SQL only".

Code (flagged lines marked >>):

       2 | import sqlite3
       3 | 
       4 | log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
       5 | USERS_TABLE = "users"
       6 |

      10 | 
      11 | 
      12 | def find_user(request):
      13 |     user_id = request.args["id"]
      14 |     cur = get_connection().cursor()
>>    15 |     cur.execute("SELECT name, email FROM users WHERE id = '" + user_id + "'")
      16 |     row = cur.fetchone()
      17 |     print("found user", row)
      18 |     return row
      19 | 
      20 |

      23 |     cur.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {USERS_TABLE}")
      24 |     return cur.fetchone()[0]
      25 | 
      26 | 
      27 | def rename_user(user_id, new_name):
</untrusted_code>

Why the reviewer kept it: Line 15 builds the SQL by concatenating `user_id`, which comes from `request.args["id"]` (external HTTP input), directly into the query string instead of using a bound parameter, creating a SQL injection path.

response.text: {"explanation": "Line 15 concatenates `user_id`, taken straight from `request.args[\"id\"]`, into the SQL text, so a crafted id can alter the query (SQL injection). The fix is to pass the value as a bound parameter with `?` placeholder and a tuple to `cur.execute`, which the policy requires for any external value.", "quote": "SQL must be built with parameters or an ORM, never by concatenating or formatting strings with values that come from outside the program.", "fix_code": "    cur.execute(\"SELECT name, email FROM users WHERE id = ?\", (user_id,))", "fix_note": "The `?` placeholder also removes the need for the surrounding single quotes, since sqlite3 binds the value with the correct type."}
